title: Parameterized Constructors
summary: Pass custom arguments at the moment of object creation so every object is born fully formed and unique.
learningObjectives: Learn to declare constructors that accept parameters
Pass arguments through the 'new ClassName(arg1, arg2)' syntax
Map incoming parameter values directly to instance variables
Enforce required fields during object instantiation
expectedOutcomes: Ability to write clean parameterized constructors in Java
Eliminate manual field assignments when creating objects with specific data

activities.title: Practical Context: Flexible Object Initialization with Arguments

analogy.headline: You don't buy a blank cup of hot water and then figure out the coffee later
analogy.story:
When you walk up to a coffee shop counter, you don't say: *"Give me an empty paper cup, and in 5 minutes I'll come back and ask for coffee beans, and in 10 minutes I'll ask for milk."*

Instead, you place your exact order right at the counter:
*"Large Caramel Macchiato with Oat Milk, please!"*

The barista takes those exact parameters and hands you a finished, customized coffee beverage ready to drink!

A **Parameterized Constructor** works the same way: you pass the exact ingredients (name, price, age) right into `new ClassName(...)`, and Java hands you an object that is fully customized from the very first millisecond.
analogy.keyTakeaway: A parameterized constructor accepts arguments during 'new ClassName(...)', guaranteeing that the object is born with specific, meaningful data.

activities.content:
In production software, objects must be configured with custom data values at creation time.

Creating an object and then setting each field manually through multiple assignment statements is verbose and risks leaving objects partially configured.

Parameterized constructors accept values as parameters during instantiation, guaranteeing complete setup in a single atomic step.

activities.title: Parameterized Constructors: Definition, Syntax, and Custom Initialization

keyTakeaways: A parameterized constructor declares parameter variables in parentheses: 'ClassName(type param1, type param2)'
Arguments passed to 'new' are received by parameters and assigned to instance fields
It prevents the creation of empty, half-initialized objects with missing data
Different objects created with different arguments hold independent data in memory

activities.title: A Real-World Product Catalog Example
activities.description: Each product receives distinct data during instantiation. The constructor cleanly guarantees that no product can be created without a name, price, and stock count.

activities.title: Example 2: Flight Reservation Ticket Entity
activities.description: Notice how all flight details are bundled atomically. You cannot buy a boarding pass without specifying the flight, passenger, seat, and luggage weight.

questions.prompt: What makes a constructor 'parameterized'?
options: It is marked with the 'param' keyword
It accepts one or more arguments inside its parentheses
It can only be called from inside a method
It returns a parameterized generic type
questions.explanation: A parameterized constructor has one or more parameters in its signature to accept initialization data.

hints.hint: Look at the parentheses: do they have parameters?

questions.prompt: Given 'class Box { Box(int w, int h) { } }', how do you create an instance in Java?
options: Box b = new Box();
Box b = new Box(10, 20);
Box b = Box.create(10, 20);
Box b = new (10, 20) Box;
questions.explanation: Because Box defines a constructor taking two integers, you must pass two matching integer arguments: new Box(10, 20).

hints.hint: Pass the arguments inside the parentheses of new Box(...).

questions.prompt: What happens if you pass a String where an int is expected: 'new Box("wide", 20)'?
options: Java converts the String to a number automatically
The program compiles but crashes at runtime
A compilation error occurs: argument types do not match the constructor signature
Java creates a half-box in memory
questions.explanation: Java is strongly-typed. Argument types must match constructor parameter types exactly, or compilation fails.

hints.hint: Type safety is enforced at compile time.

options: null
Matrix
t
Compile error
questions.explanation: "Matrix" is passed into parameter t, which is then assigned to instance field title.

hints.hint: Follow the assignment: title = t.

questions.prompt: Why are parameterized constructors preferred over creating an empty object and setting fields manually?
options: They guarantee objects cannot be instantiated in an incomplete or invalid state
They reduce memory consumption by 90%
They make the Java bytecode compatible with C++
They allow fields to be declared without types
questions.explanation: Parameterized constructors enforce that all required data must be supplied up front before the object can exist.

hints.hint: Preventing incomplete objects is key.

questions.prompt: Can a parameterized constructor take multiple parameters of different data types (e.g. String, int, double)?
options: No, all parameters must be of the same type
Yes, a constructor can accept any valid combination of Java data types
Only up to 2 parameters are permitted in Java
Yes, but only if they are primitive types
questions.explanation: A constructor can accept any number and combination of primitive and reference types.

hints.hint: Just like a method signature, types can be mixed.

options: Point p1 = new Point(5, 10);
Point p2 = new Point(0, 0);
Point p3 = new Point();
Point p4 = new Point(-3, 8);
questions.explanation: Because a parameterized constructor was defined, the default no-arg constructor was not generated. Point() is undefined.

hints.hint: Is there a constructor that takes zero arguments?

questions.prompt: What happens inside memory when 'new Student("Aarav", 20)' is called?
options: The parameters are discarded and fields remain null and 0
A new heap object is allocated, and the constructor copies "Aarav" and 20 into the object's instance fields
The class definition itself is permanently overwritten with "Aarav"
The JVM re-compiles the Student class file
questions.explanation: The constructor runs in the context of the newly created heap instance, writing values into its fields.

hints.hint: Constructor assigns parameter values to the new instance's fields.

questions.prompt: If parameter names match field names exactly without 'this' (e.g. name = name), what happens?
options: Java assigns the value correctly anyway
The parameter assigns to itself, leaving the instance field uninitialized (shadowing trap)
The code refuses to compile with a syntax error
The computer screen flashes red
questions.explanation: Without 'this', the local parameter shadows the instance field, so 'name = name' assigns the parameter to itself!

hints.hint: This is the classic variable shadowing trap.

questions.prompt: Can you call methods from inside a parameterized constructor?
options: Yes, a constructor can call methods to perform validation or complex setup
No, methods cannot be invoked until the main method finishes
Only static methods can be called
Only private methods can be called
questions.explanation: Constructors are executable code blocks and can call methods to validate parameters or perform initial calculations.

hints.hint: A constructor can execute any valid Java statements.

interviewQA.question: What is a parameterized constructor, and what problem does it solve?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: A parameterized constructor is a constructor that accepts arguments to initialize an object's instance variables with specific values at the moment of creation. It solves the problem of creating uninitialized or inconsistent objects by forcing the caller to provide required data up front.
keyPoints: Accepts one or more arguments
Guarantees required state is populated at birth
Eliminates repetitive post-instantiation field assignment
commonMistakes: Thinking parameterized constructors only set values. They can also validate input before setting fields.

interviewQA.question: Can you have both a no-arg constructor and a parameterized constructor in the same class?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes, absolutely! Having both allows callers the flexibility to create default objects or provide custom values. This is known as constructor overloading.
keyPoints: Multiple constructors can coexist in one class
Enables flexible object construction patterns
commonMistakes: Assuming Java only allows one constructor per class.

interviewQA.question: What happens if you pass null as an argument to a reference type parameter in a constructor?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java accepts null without issue at compile time because null is a valid literal for any reference type. However, if the constructor or subsequent methods attempt to call methods on that null field, a NullPointerException will be thrown at runtime.
keyPoints: null is legally accepted by reference parameters
Can lead to NullPointerException if not validated
commonMistakes: Believing the compiler rejects null arguments automatically.

interviewQA.question: Can a parameterized constructor have validation logic (e.g. checking for negative numbers)?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes! A constructor can contain if-statements, throw exceptions, or clamp values. For instance, if an opening balance is negative, a constructor can reset it to zero or throw an IllegalArgumentException to ensure data integrity.
keyPoints: Constructors can validate incoming arguments
Guarantees the object is always valid upon creation
commonMistakes: Treating constructors as purely passive assignment blocks.

interviewQA.question: How does Java differentiate which constructor to execute when an object is instantiated?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Java uses the argument list passed to 'new'. It matches the number, types, and order of the arguments against the available constructor signatures at compile time.
keyPoints: Resolved at compile time
Matches argument count, types, and sequence
commonMistakes: Thinking Java picks constructors at runtime based on object names.

interviewQA.question: Is it possible to copy values from one object to another using a constructor?
interviewQA.expectedAnswer: Yes! This is known as a Copy Constructor in Java. It takes an existing instance of the same class as its parameter and copies all its field values into the new instance.
keyPoints: Copy constructor accepts an object of the same class
Creates a duplicate object with identical state
commonMistakes: Thinking Java has a built-in copy keyword like C++.

practiceProblems.title: Create a Book with Title and Author
practiceProblems.description:
Create a `Book` class that takes custom values upon instantiation.

• Class `Book`:
  - Fields: `String title`, `String author`
  - Constructor `Book(String bTitle, String bAuthor)`: sets `title = bTitle` and `author = bAuthor`
  - Method `void printInfo()`: prints `[title] by [author]`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `Book b = new Book("Atomic Habits", "James Clear");`
  - Call `b.printInfo()`

Target Console Output:
Atomic Habits by James Clear

  - Constructor `Book(String bTitle, String bAuthor)`: sets `title = bTitle` and `author = bAuthor`
  - Method `void printInfo()`: prints `[title] by [author]`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `Book b = new Book("Atomic Habits", "James Clear");`
  - Call `b.printInfo()`

Target Console Output:
Atomic Habits by James Clear
practiceProblems.hint: Pass parameters to constructor during new: new Book("Atomic Habits", "James Clear").
hints: Assign title = bTitle; author = bAuthor; in constructor.

practiceProblems.title: Instantiate Two Movie Tickets
practiceProblems.description:
Model a movie ticketing system where each ticket is created with specific details.

• Class `Ticket`:
  - Fields: `String movieName`, `String seatNumber`, `double price`
  - Constructor `Ticket(String movie, String seat, double p)`: assigns all 3 fields
  - Method `void printTicket(int ticketNum)`: prints `Ticket [ticketNum]: [movieName] [[seatNumber]] - $[price]`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create ticket 1: `"Inception"`, `"A-12"`, `12.5`
  - Create ticket 2: `"Interstellar"`, `"B-05"`, `15.0`
  - Print both ticket summaries on separate lines

Target Console Output:
Ticket 1: Inception [A-12] - $12.5
Ticket 2: Interstellar [B-05] - $15.0

practiceProblems.title: Build a Rectangle with Area Calculation
practiceProblems.description:
Construct a `Rectangle` requiring exact dimensions at creation time.

• Class `Rectangle`:
  - Fields: `double width`, `double height`
  - Constructor `Rectangle(double w, double h)`: sets fields to arguments
  - Method `double getArea()`: returns `width * height`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `Rectangle r = new Rectangle(4.5, 2.0);`
  - Print: `Area: [r.getArea()]`

Target Console Output:
Area: 9.0

practiceProblems.title: Validate Positive Balance in Constructor
practiceProblems.description:
Use constructor logic to prevent illegal states, like starting with a negative bank balance.

• Class `Account`:
  - Fields: `String owner`, `double balance`
  - Constructor `Account(String o, double b)`:
    - Sets `owner = o`
    - If `b < 0`, sets `balance = 0.0`; otherwise sets `balance = b`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `Account acc = new Account("Charlie", -50.0);`
  - Print: `Account: [acc.owner] | Balance: $[acc.balance]`

Target Console Output:
Account: Charlie | Balance: $0.0
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Use constructor logic to prevent illegal states, like starting with a negative bank balance.

• Class `Account`:
  - Fields: `String owner`, `double balance`
  - Constructor `Account(String o, double b)`:
    - Sets `owner = o`
    - If `b < 0`, sets `balance = 0.0`; otherwise sets `balance = b`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - Create `Account acc = new Account("Charlie", -50.0);`
  - Print: `Account: [acc.owner] | Balance: $[acc.balance]`

Target Console Output:
Account: Charlie | Balance: $0.0
practiceProblems.hint: Use an if-else check inside the constructor: if (b < 0) balance = 0.0; else balance = b;.
hints: Constructors can validate data before initializing object state.

practiceProblems.title: Copy Constructor Pattern
practiceProblems.description:
Write a copy constructor that copies the fields of an existing object into a brand new object.

• Class `Point`:
  - Fields: `int x`, `int y`
  - Constructor 1: `Point(int px, int py)` sets `x = px` and `y = py`
  - Constructor 2 (Copy): `Point(Point other)` sets `x = other.x` and `y = other.y`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - `Point p1 = new Point(10, 20);`
  - `Point p2 = new Point(p1);`
  - Print: `Clone Point -> X: [p2.x], Y: [p2.y]`

Target Console Output:
Clone Point -> X: 10, Y: 20

  - Constructor 2 (Copy): `Point(Point other)` sets `x = other.x` and `y = other.y`
• In `Main.main()`:
  - `Point p1 = new Point(10, 20);`
  - `Point p2 = new Point(p1);`
  - Print: `Clone Point -> X: [p2.x], Y: [p2.y]`

Target Console Output:
Clone Point -> X: 10, Y: 20
practiceProblems.hint: Inside Point(Point other), assign this.x = other.x; this.y = other.y;.
hints: A copy constructor takes another instance of the exact same class as a parameter.
